blocks.text: Here are the basic types of polarization of light.
When the electric field vector oscillates in a single plane, the light is said to be linearly polarized (Fig. 8.4a). An example is light passing through a polarizing filter, as in sunglasses.

When the electric field rotates circularly, either clockwise (right-handed) or anticlockwise (left-handed), the light is said to be circularly polarized (Fig. 8.4b). An example given in the book is light reflected off a CD (Compact Disc) or DVD (Digital Versatile Disc).

A combination of linear and circular polarization, in which the electric field vector traces an elliptical path, is called elliptical polarization. In elliptical polarization (Fig. 8.4c) the two components of the electric field, E_x and E_y, are not equal, and/or they differ in phase by an arbitrary angle theta. An example is light passing through a stress plate or a waveplate.

blocks.prompt: Write down some applications of plane polarized and circularly polarized light (constructed response 8.1).
blocks.explanation: Plane polarized light: polarized sunglasses and camera filters that cut glare, LCD screens, the polarizer-analyzer arrangement for detecting polarization, measuring the concentration of sugar solutions through optical activity, and stress analysis of materials. Circular and elliptical polarization arise when light is reflected from surfaces such as a CD or DVD or passes through a stress plate or waveplate, and polarization of light is used in optical communication systems and in astronomy.

items: Linear: E in one plane (polarizing filter, sunglasses). Circular: E rotates clockwise (right-handed) or anticlockwise (left-handed) (CD or DVD reflection). Elliptical: E traces an ellipse, E_x and E_y unequal and/or out of phase by theta (stress plate, waveplate).
